issues.issue: The provision fixes effectiveness on "the first date that all the parties have signed the signature page" yet also declares the offer and Agreement "void" unless employment commences by the April 16, 2012 start date, leaving unclear which event controls if signature and commencement do not align. "Successful completion of all required pre-employment screenings" is likewise left to be judged by no stated standard.

"You are expected to complete satisfactorily all assignments and training obligations" states an expectation rather than a covenant, so whether it imposes an enforceable duty is open. "Satisfactorily" is measured only by Wells Fargo Advisors' "sole discretion" language applied to the materials, not to performance.

"At least initially, you will be eligible for overtime pay" fixes no period and no event ending eligibility, so the duration of the overtime entitlement is indeterminate on the face of the clause. The phrase also leaves open whether eligibility is a contractual promise or merely a description of current classification.

Overtime eligibility is made to end "[o]nce your title changes," while Paragraph 3 grants overtime eligibility "at least initially" — the two do not say whether the cut-off is the title change, graduation, or attainment of the Series 7, Series 66 and state insurance licenses. The trigger is stated in Paragraph 4 as a compound of four conditions with no statement of what happens if some but not all are met.

"May lead to consequences, up to and including termination from the Training Program" names no determinate consequence and no standard for choosing among them. "Failure to behave professionally" is likewise undefined.

The closing sentence preserves all "Wells Fargo human resources policies and programs" and "compliance or regulatory guidelines" as binding on the employee, which cannot be squared with Paragraph 20's statement that this Agreement "constitutes the entire understanding" and Paragraph 8's requirement that changes be signed by a Regional President. A court would have to decide whether unwritten policies form part of the parties' bargain.

The at-will promise that Wells Fargo Advisors "may terminate the employment of any employee at its discretion at any time for any reason" sits against Paragraph 10(a), which makes the employee repay Training Costs if "terminated for any reason at any time," and Paragraph 10(b)(i), which conditions forgiveness on five years of continuous employment the employer can unilaterally prevent. Whether the repayment obligation survives an employer-initiated discharge is the construction question.

"This Agreement serves only as a synopsis of the compensation and other arrangements" cannot be squared with Paragraph 20's entire-agreement clause or with the substantive covenants in Paragraphs 10, 11 and 12; a synopsis of other arrangements and an integrated contract are different instruments. A court would have to decide whether the operative obligations are these words or the plans and policies they purport to summarize.

The proviso exempting "changes to any Wells Fargo Advisors compensation or benefit plans or policies" from the signed-writing requirement leaves open whether the employer may, by amending a plan, alter terms stated in the Agreement itself — such as the overtime eligibility in Paragraph 3 or the compensation mechanics in Paragraph 9. The exception's boundary against the rule it qualifies is not drawn.

"Wells Fargo Advisors shall be liable to you only for compensation earned and received by Wells Fargo Advisors" makes the firm's receipt, not the employee's performance, the measure of what is owed, and "any deficit balances (unrelated to the offset of the draw)" is nowhere defined. What counts as revenue "fronted" or "advanced" and recoverable in the month of termination is left to be construed.

The paragraph uses two different cut-offs — employment "on the date such payments are received by Wells Fargo Advisors" and employment "on the applicable payout date" — without saying which governs eligibility for the same monthly compensation. Neither "payout date" nor the receipt date is defined in the Agreement.

The dollar amounts of the Training Costs the employee promises to repay are illegible/blank in subparagraphs (i) and (ii), so the essential quantum of the obligation is not stated in the instrument. A court would have to determine the amount, if any, from outside the document.

The flat duty to repay when "terminated for any reason at any time" is expressly subject to Paragraph 10(b), whose exception (ii)(A) turns on conduct during the year AFTER termination, so the obligation cannot be fixed at termination as 10(a) states. Whether repayment is due immediately or only after the one-year look-forward has run is the conflict.

Forgiveness here requires five continuous years measured from the later of graduation and full registration, while Paragraph 10(c) amortizes the same Training Costs to zero forty-eight months after the start of the second year of employment as a New FA. The two run from different dates and can produce different outcomes for the same termination.

"Competitive Organization or Entity" is defined "as including, but not be limited to" a list of financial firms closed by the catch-all "any other person, firm, corporation, or entity that competes with Wells Fargo Advisors," so the class is bounded neither by the enumeration nor by any definition of competition. Whether the catch-all is read ejusdem generis with the listed securities and insurance businesses decides who the ex-employee may work for.

The 1/48 monthly reduction "beginning with the first month of the second year" of employment as a New FA does not say whether the reductions accumulate or when they stop, and it is measured from employment start while Paragraph 10(b)(i) measures forgiveness from graduation and full registration. The two schedules cannot both fix the date the obligation disappears.

Setoff is to be effected "in the calculation of your monthly compensation," but under Paragraphs 3 and 4 a New FA is paid a bi-weekly salary and becomes eligible for monthly compensation only on graduation, so the mechanism has nothing to operate on for a trainee. Whether the firm may instead deduct from salary is not addressed.

Category (ii), "[a]ll records and other documents made and/or maintained in connection with Wells Fargo Advisors business," is not limited to confidential material and swallows the "confidential information or trade secrets" limit of category (i). The scope of "Confidential Information and Documents" is therefore indeterminate.

The surrender obligation attaches to "any Confidential Records or Documents," a term that appears nowhere else and does not match "Confidential Information and Documents" defined in Paragraph 11(a). Which body of material must be returned is left to construction.

The prohibition reaches any client "that you had contact with or otherwise learned of" during employment, and "otherwise learned of" has no discernible boundary; "solicit or cause or permit to be solicited" is likewise undefined. Whether announcements or client-initiated contact fall within it is the construction question.

The sentence's final clause — "or discontinuing his or her employment with Wells Fargo Advisors" — has no verb to attach to, so the grammar does not say whether inducing an employee to quit (without recruiting for another firm) is prohibited. The catch-all "any other lines of business in which Wells Fargo Advisors or any of its affiliates is engaged" further leaves the covered field unbounded.

"[Y]ou will be expected to contribute" states an expectation, not a promise, and the amount is "determined after a consultation" with management with no formula or cap. Whether this creates an enforceable payment obligation, and in what sum, cannot be read off the words.

"You will be accountable for errors incurred from orders entered by you or by anyone on your behalf" does not say whether accountability is financial, disciplinary, or both, and "anyone on your behalf" is undefined. The measure of the employee's exposure for another's order is therefore open.

"Net Eligible Revenue" is capitalized as a defined term but is defined nowhere in the Agreement, existing only in the separately modifiable New FA Compensation Plan referred to in Paragraph 3. The size of the adjustment therefore cannot be determined from the instrument.

This disclosure says the employee agrees to arbitrate disputes "between you and Wells Fargo Advisors, or a client, or any other person," whereas the operative agreement in Paragraph 14(b) covers only controversies "arising between you and Wells Fargo Advisors." Which scope binds — and whether clients and third parties may compel arbitration — is a direct conflict within Paragraph 14.

Statutory discrimination claims are said to be "REQUIRED" to be arbitrated, yet the following bullet excludes claims processed under a different administrative procedure and claims within the state employment-insurance system, including retaliation-adjacent matters. Whether a statutory claim falling in both bullets must be arbitrated is unresolved.

"[C]laims under the National Labor Relations Act" is placed inside the parenthetical illustrating "State unemployment insurance" ("i.e., unemployment compensation, workers' compensation, work disability compensation or claims under the National Labor Relations Act"), so the punctuation leaves unclear whether federal NLRA claims are excluded from arbitration at all. The unclosed structure of the parenthetical changes the reach of the exclusion.

"[O]r similar administrative determination" has no defined boundary, so which agency dispositions convert an administrative charge into an arbitrable claim is left open. The bullet also does not say what happens to the charge if the agency itself sues.

The sentence reads "as provided by the rules of the arbitration forum in the claim is filed," omitting words ("in which") so that the clause does not parse. Which forum's rules govern panel composition must be supplied by construction.

The statement that "a claim that is ineligible for arbitration may be brought to court" cannot be squared with Paragraph 14(b), which provides that a claim FINRA does not accept goes instead to the American Arbitration Association, and with the jury-waiver bullet giving up the right to sue. Whether a FINRA-ineligible claim goes to court or to the AAA is a direct conflict.

The fallback sends non-accepted claims to "the American Arbitration Association pursuant to its Securities Arbitration Rules, effective May 1, 1993," a rule set that no longer exists, and "does not accept" is undefined (refusal, ineligibility, or a rule barring the claim form). The mechanics of the fallback forum therefore cannot be applied as written.

The operative clause covers only disputes "arising between you and Wells Fargo Advisors," while the Paragraph 14(a) disclosures state the employee arbitrates disputes with "a client, or any other person" and that ineligible claims may be brought to court. Which of the two governs the scope and the fallback forum is squarely in issue.

The carve-out lets Wells Fargo Advisors go to "any court of competent jurisdiction" "[n]otwithstanding any other provision," which cannot be squared with Paragraph 14(b)'s mandatory FINRA arbitration and the Paragraph 14(a) bullet by which the employee gives up the right to sue in court. Whether the employer alone escapes arbitration, and for which claims connected to Paragraphs 11 and 12, is the question.

The survival list names "indemnification obligations," but the Agreement contains no indemnification provision — the closest is the contribution expectation in Paragraph 13(a). What obligation survives under that label can only be settled by reading the instrument as a whole.

The clause permits Wells Fargo Advisors to assign the Agreement but says nothing about whether an assignee may enforce the Paragraph 11 and 12 restrictive covenants against the employee or whether the assignor remains bound. The consequences of assignment are simply not addressed.

The clause selects Missouri law to "construe[] and enforce[]" an agreement for employment in a New York branch office, without saying whether it reaches the enforceability of the Paragraph 12 restrictive covenants or statutory wage claims as opposed to contract interpretation. Its scope against the law of the employee's place of work is the construction question.

The second sentence says invalidity "shall not affect the validity or unenforceability of the remaining Provisions," which as written preserves their UNenforceability — the opposite of the saving purpose stated in the first sentence. The word error changes the meaning of the severability promise.

The clause preserves the right to enforce "any other breach of the same or any other covenant," and so is silent on — and arguably concedes — waiver of the very breach forgone. It also runs only in Wells Fargo Advisors' favor, leaving the employee's forbearance ungoverned.

"[T]he RESTRICTIVE COVENANTS" is capitalized as though defined, but the Agreement never identifies which paragraphs they are; only the heading of Paragraph 19 and the headings of Paragraphs 11 and 12 suggest it, and Paragraph 17 says captions "shall not affect in any way the meaning or interpretation." What the employee acknowledged reading is therefore not fixed by the text.

The entire-agreement statement cannot be squared with Paragraph 8, which says the Agreement "serves only as a synopsis" of arrangements found elsewhere, or with Paragraph 6, which preserves Wells Fargo human resources policies and compliance guidelines as binding. Whether the New FA Compensation Plan and those policies are part of the parties' agreement turns on which provision controls.

This general survival sentence sits against Paragraph 15, which already specifies that the confidentiality provisions, post-employment restrictions and indemnification obligations survive; whether Paragraph 15's enumeration limits what survives or Paragraph 20 extends survival to every clause is unresolved. The test "require survival ... in order to give full legal effect thereto" supplies no independent criterion.
